verifiedClaims.claim: The Most Dangerous Intersections and Roads in Columbia, South Carolina
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Crash VOLUME supports a 'highest-crash' framing: Richland County ranked 3rd of 46 counties in total collisions (12,068) and 2nd in fatal collisions (60) in 2024. Crash RATE does not: Richland's 2024 mileage death rate was 1.451 and Lexington's 1.589 deaths per 100 million VMT, both below the statewide 1.68. Of the post's seven numbered locations, only three appear in the SCDPS county Top-5 intersection tables (I-20/I-26, I-20/Broad River Rd, SC-12/I-77 — the last only in 2023).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Office of Highway Safety and Justice Programs, South Carolina Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition (latest), Part VI county tables: Lexington County p. 148, Richland County p. 164; Part II interstates p. 28
verifiedClaims.note: NOT a patcher-editable surface (title is not in body.html) — for the owner. 'Most Dangerous' is defensible only as 'highest-crash by count' and only for the SCDPS-listed interchanges; the surface-street intersections (Two Notch/Sparkleberry, Assembly/Gervais, Garners Ferry/Leesburg, Broad River/Bush River) have no published counts behind them. Suggested title: "Columbia, SC's Highest-Crash Intersections and Roads: A Driver's Guide". If the title stays, the body must define 'dangerous' as SCDPS crash counts (see edits). Mileage death rates: Fact Book 2024 Part I summary (state MDR 1.68) and county Statistics tables (pp. 149, 165).

verifiedClaims.claim: Columbia, South Carolina sits at the crossroads of three major interstate highways — I-20, I-26, and I-77 — making it one of the busiest and most collision-prone metropolitan areas in the Southeast.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Richland County: 3rd of 46 SC counties in total collisions in 2023 and 2024, 2nd in fatal collisions in 2024 (5th in 2023). No Southeast-wide metro comparison exists in SCDPS, SCDOT or NHTSA publications.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Office of Highway Safety and Justice Programs, South Carolina Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition (latest), Part VI county tables: Lexington County p. 148, Richland County p. 164; Part II interstates p. 28
verifiedClaims.note: Interstates verified (I-126 also enters). 'One of the busiest and most collision-prone metropolitan areas in the Southeast' is untraceable — no regional ranking was found. Replace the clause with the in-state fact: '...— and Richland County consistently ranks among South Carolina's highest-crash counties.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Richland County, where Columbia is located, recorded 12,450 traffic collisions in 2023 — the third-highest total of South Carolina’s 46 counties, behind only Greenville and Charleston — including 58 fatal collisions in which 60 people died
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2024 (latest): Richland County 12,068 collisions — 3rd of 46, behind Greenville (16,478) and Charleston (15,802) — including 60 fatal collisions in which 64 people died; 2nd in the state for fatal collisions. 2023 figures in the post (12,450; 58 fatal; 60 killed; 3rd) verified exactly against the 2023 edition.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Office of Highway Safety and Justice Programs, South Carolina Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition (latest), Part VI county tables: Lexington County p. 148, Richland County p. 164; Part II interstates p. 28
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate for 2023 but one edition stale. Replace with: 'Richland County, where most of Columbia is located, recorded 12,068 traffic collisions in 2024 — the third-highest total of South Carolina's 46 counties, behind only Greenville and Charleston — including 60 fatal collisions in which 64 people died' and repoint the link to the 2024 Fact Book (link text 'SCDPS Traffic Collision Fact Book, 2024 edition'). Lexington County, the other half of the metro, had 8,269 collisions and 55 deaths in 2024 (6th of 46). 2023 source: https://scdps.sc.gov/sites/scdps/files/Documents/ohsjp/fact%20book/2023%20Fact%20Book.pdf

verifiedClaims.currentValue: By count: Richland 3rd in collisions, 2nd in fatal collisions (2024). By rate: Richland (1.451) and Lexington (1.589) below the statewide mileage death rate (1.68).

verifiedClaims.claim: Three major interstates converge within the city limits, and the resulting interchange complexes — particularly the I-20/I-26 junction known as "Malfunction Junction" — handle traffic volumes that regularly exceed their design capacity.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: SCDOT: the interchange 'no longer meets the demands of modern traffic'; Carolina Crossroads is rebuilding the I-20/I-26/I-126 corridor (construction began Nov. 2021; Phases 1–2 complete 2025; Phase 3C I-20 widening and Saluda River bridge replacement under construction in 2026; the I-20/I-26 system interchange itself, Phase 3E, still in design; substantial completion mid-2030s). I-26 carries 143,900 vehicles/day between St. Andrews Rd and I-20 (SCDOT 2025 AADT).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDOT Carolina Crossroads general handout and FAQ (April 2026)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Within the city limits' is not verified (no source places the I-20/I-26 interchange inside Columbia's corporate limits; it is commonly described as at St. Andrews) — say 'converge around the city'. 'Regularly exceed their design capacity' has no published capacity study; use SCDOT's own words. Suggested: "Three major interstates converge around the city, and SCDOT says the I-20/I-26 junction known as 'Malfunction Junction' 'no longer meets the demands of modern traffic' — about 144,000 vehicles a day use I-26 just north of it (SCDOT, 2025)." AADT: https://www.scdot.org/content/dam/scdot-legacy/travel/pdf/trafficcounts/2025/LEXINGTON.pdf

verifiedClaims.claim: Many of the city's busiest arterials — Two Notch Road, Broad River Road, Assembly Street, and Garners Ferry Road — were designed for much lower traffic volumes than they carry today.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2025 AADT: Two Notch Rd (US-1) 34,000 near I-20; Garners Ferry Rd (US-76) 50,200 near Leesburg Rd; Broad River Rd (US-176) 23,400–28,900 near Bush River Rd; Assembly St (SC-48) 20,400–25,400 near Gervais St.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDOT Average Daily Traffic for Richland County, 2025 AADT (generated 2026-03-13)
verifiedClaims.note: No design-volume records were found for these arterials; 'designed for much lower traffic volumes' is untraceable. Economical fix: "Many of the city's busiest arterials — Two Notch Road, Broad River Road, Assembly Street, and Garners Ferry Road — carry 20,000 to 50,000 vehicles a day (SCDOT, 2025)."

verifiedClaims.currentValue: SCDPS Top 5 Intersections, 2024 — Richland: I-20 at US-176/Broad River Rd 224; I-26 at US-176/Broad River Rd 170; I-20 at SC-215/Monticello Rd 116; SC-48/Bluff Rd at I-77 107; I-20 at I-26 95. Lexington: I-26 at S-671/Piney Grove Rd 163; I-26 at S-36/St. Andrews Rd 161; I-26 at US-378/Sunset Blvd 154; I-20 at I-26 124; US-21/Charleston Hwy at I-26 122 (2 fatal). 2023 — Richland: I-20 at US-176 229; I-26 at US-176 199; SC-12/Percival Rd at I-77 116; I-20 at SC-215 110; SC-48 at I-77 107. Every SCDPS-listed location is an interstate interchange. Road names from SCDOT 2025 AADT station descriptions (US 176 = Broad River Rd, SC 215 = Monticello Rd, SC 48 = Bluff Rd at I-77, SC 12 = Percival Rd, S-36 = Saint Andrews Rd, S-671 = Piney Grove Rd, US 378 = Sunset Blvd, US 21 = Charleston Hwy). SCDPS caveat: rankings rely on route names the officer enters. Replace with: "SCDPS publishes each county's five highest-crash intersections every year. The first three locations below appear in those tables; the surface-street intersections that follow are busy crossroads for which the state publishes no intersection-level counts." Also reorder so I-20 at Broad River Road is No. 1 (or remove the numbers, which read as a ranking).

verifiedClaims.claim: 2. I-20 and US-76 (Broad River Road)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2024: 'I-20 at US-176' — US-176 is Broad River Road (SCDOT station 2033 'US 176 (BROAD RIVER RD)') — was Richland County's No. 1 intersection with 224 collisions, 0 fatal, 67 injured, and second statewide behind I-85 at S-492 in Greenville (277). 2023: 229 collisions, 1 fatal (1 killed), 56 injured — also Richland's No. 1 and second statewide. Broad River Road also meets I-26 at Richland's No. 2 intersection ('I-26 at US-176': 170 collisions in 2024, 199 in 2023). I-20 has no interchange with US-76. The I-20/Broad River Road interchange was rebuilt as Carolina Crossroads Phase 2, 'fully operational in fall 2025' (SCDOT) — the 2023–2024 counts were recorded during construction.

verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Office of Highway Safety and Justice Programs, South Carolina Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition (latest), Part VI county tables: Lexington County p. 148, Richland County p. 164; Part II interstates p. 28

verifiedClaims.claim: Columbia's nightlife districts along Main Street and in Five Points contribute to a significant number of impaired-driving intersection crashes during late-night hours.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: No district-level DUI crash data
verifiedClaims.note: Untraceable location attribution. Soften: "Impaired driving: Late-night traffic around Columbia's nightlife districts, including Main Street and Five Points, raises the risk of impaired-driving crashes."

verifiedClaims.claim: Several of Columbia's most crash-prone intersections have known design deficiencies — including inadequate sight lines, confusing lane configurations, and insufficient signage — that contribute to collisions. When a dangerous road condition causes a crash, the responsible government agency may bear liability.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-78-60(15): 'Governmental entities are not liable for the design of highways and other public ways.' Liability for a sign or signal exists only for its 'absence, condition, or malfunction' not corrected within a reasonable time after actual or constructive notice; failure to initially place a sign is not actionable when discretionary. Highway defects are actionable only if not corrected after actual or constructive notice. Caps $300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence (§ 15-78-120).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 15-78-60(15), 15-78-120 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Known design deficiencies' at named intersections is unsourced, and design is expressly immune. Replace the bullet text with: "Dangerous road conditions: When a malfunctioning signal, missing sign, or road defect that the responsible agency knew or should have known about contributes to a crash, the agency may be liable under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act — but not for the highway's design itself (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(15))."

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina gives accident victims three years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-3-530 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: § 15-3-530(5). Wrongful death runs from death (§ 15-3-530(6)); minors tolled by § 15-3-40 (not on page; no edit). Government defendants: two years (§ 15-78-110) — stated in FAQ 6.

verifiedClaims.claim: You can recover compensation if you are less than 51% at fault for the accident, but your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Modified comparative fault (plaintiff's negligence not greater than defendants'). CourtListener returns 202 to curl (bot gate); authority reused from sibling packs 4624/4644.

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 56-5-2310 through § 56-5-2350 govern right-of-way rules at South Carolina intersections.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 56-5-2310 vehicle on the left yields to vehicle on the right when arriving at approximately the same time; § 56-5-2320 left-turning vehicle yields to oncoming traffic; § 56-5-2330 stop and yield signs; § 56-5-2350 entering from a non-roadway. (No § 56-5-2340 in the current code.) Signals: § 56-5-970.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-2310 to -2350 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: Range citation accurate; the left-turn example is § 56-5-2320.

verifiedClaims.claim: Violations of these statutes — such as failing to yield to oncoming traffic when making a left turn — constitute negligence per se, meaning the violation itself can serve as proof of fault in your injury claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-2320, 56-5-6160 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: Overstated: under SC law a statutory violation is negligence per se, but the plaintiff must still prove it proximately caused the injury; and evidence of a traffic conviction is inadmissible in a civil action (§ 56-5-6160). Suggested: "...constitute negligence per se, which can establish the other driver was negligent — though you must still show the violation caused your injuries." (Chapman v. Associated Transport, 218 S.C. 554 (1951) is the usual cite; opinion host 403'd, not cited.)

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina requires drivers to carry uninsured motorist coverage under S.C. Code § 38-77-150, which protects you if the at-fault driver has no insurance or insufficient coverage to pay for your injuries.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 38-77-150: every policy must include UM coverage (at § 38-77-140 minimums, $25,000/$50,000/$25,000). Coverage for an at-fault driver with 'insufficient coverage' is UNDERinsured motorist (UIM) coverage, which insurers must offer but drivers may decline (§ 38-77-160).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150, 38-77-160 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: Conflates UM and UIM. Replace: "...under S.C. Code § 38-77-150, which protects you if the at-fault driver has no insurance or flees the scene. Underinsured motorist coverage, for a driver whose limits are too low, is optional (§ 38-77-160)." The hit-and-run sentence that follows is fine (unknown-driver UM claims require a police report, § 38-77-170).

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina law requires you to notify police immediately after a crash that injures or kills anyone (S.C. Code § 56-5-1260).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-1260 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: Verified: notice 'immediately by the quickest means of communication' to local police (inside a municipality), otherwise the sheriff or Highway Patrol.

verifiedClaims.claim: If no officer investigated a crash involving injury or $1,000 or more in property damage, the driver or owner must file a written report with the DMV within 15 days (S.C. Code § 56-5-1270).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-1270 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: Verified ('one thousand dollars or more', 'within fifteen days', to the Department of Motor Vehicles, with verification of insurance). The officer's own report is the TR-310; the post does not mention FR-10, so no form fix needed. Same sentence in FAQ 5 — keep.

verifiedClaims.claim: The police report becomes key evidence in your claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-1290 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: § 56-5-1290: none of the reports required by §§ 56-5-1260 to -1280 'may be evidence of the negligence or due care of either party at the trial'. Suggested: "The police report is key to your insurance claim, although South Carolina does not allow it as evidence of fault at trial (S.C. Code § 56-5-1290)."

verifiedClaims.claim: Police accident report: The investigating officer's report includes witness statements, diagrams, citations, and a fault determination that carries significant weight in settlement negotiations.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1290, 56-5-6160 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: Fine for settlement, but add the trial caveat: "...carries significant weight in settlement negotiations, though the report itself and any traffic conviction are inadmissible as proof of fault at trial (S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1290, 56-5-6160)."

verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDOT, Freedom of Information Act FAQ
verifiedClaims.note: See previous: change 'traffic camera footage' to 'available video footage'.

verifiedClaims.note: Design is immune; notice matters for maintenance defects and sign/signal malfunctions. Change 'If road design or maintenance failures' to 'If a maintenance failure or a malfunctioning signal'.

verifiedClaims.claim: The I-20 and US-76 (Broad River Road) interchange and the I-20/I-26 junction known as “Malfunction Junction” are the two locations most consistently identified as Columbia's worst.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2024: 'I-20 at US-176' — US-176 is Broad River Road (SCDOT station 2033 'US 176 (BROAD RIVER RD)') — was Richland County's No. 1 intersection with 224 collisions, 0 fatal, 67 injured, and second statewide behind I-85 at S-492 in Greenville (277). 2023: 229 collisions, 1 fatal (1 killed), 56 injured — also Richland's No. 1 and second statewide. Broad River Road also meets I-26 at Richland's No. 2 intersection ('I-26 at US-176': 170 collisions in 2024, 199 in 2023). I-20 has no interchange with US-76. The I-20/Broad River Road interchange was rebuilt as Carolina Crossroads Phase 2, 'fully operational in fall 2025' (SCDOT) — the 2023–2024 counts were recorded during construction. 2024 (latest SCDPS edition): 'I-20 at I-26' is Lexington County's No. 4 intersection — 124 collisions, 1 fatal (1 killed), 21 injured — and Richland County's No. 5 — 95 collisions, 0 fatal, 27 injured (crashes are coded to one county, so the two rows do not overlap: 219 in all). 2023: Lexington 145 collisions, 0 fatal, 28 injured (verified); Richland 'I-20 at I-26' was not in its 2023 top five. SCDOT 2025 AADT: I-26 between St. Andrews Rd and I-20, 143,900 vehicles/day; I-26 between I-20 and I-126, 127,700; I-20 between Bush River Rd and I-26, 92,300; I-20 between I-26 and US-176 (Broad River Rd), 112,700.

The I-20/I-26 'Malfunction Junction' also ranks in both Richland's and Lexington's top five, with 219 collisions across the two counties in 2024. Both are being rebuilt under SCDOT's Carolina Crossroads program."

verifiedClaims.currentValue: SCDOT calls it 'commonly known as "Malfunction Junction"' without giving an origin; its rebuild replaces cloverleaf loops with directional ramps and adds longer, separated exits. 2024 crash severity: 1 fatal crash among 219 collisions coded to the interchange.

SCDOT says it 'no longer meets the demands of modern traffic' and is rebuilding it through the Carolina Crossroads program, which it expects to substantially complete in the mid-2030s."

verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1260, 56-5-1270 (scstatehouse.gov)
